Yeah, this has been getting noticeably worse. I asked it to help me draft a professional email last week and it spent half the response psychoanalyzing why I might be feeling anxious about sending the email. I didn't say anything about being anxious. I just wanted help with the wording.

The pattern seems to be: OpenAI got burned by the sycophancy criticism ("ChatGPT just agrees with everything"), so they over-tuned in the opposite direction. Now instead of being a yes-man, it's become that friend who took one psychology class and won't stop diagnosing everyone.

The therapy-speak creep is especially annoying when you're using it for practical tasks. If I'm asking about legal options for a friend, I don't need the model to question my friend's motivations. That's not its job. It's supposed to be a tool, not an unsolicited counselor.

I think the core issue is that RLHF training makes it really hard to find the sweet spot between "helpful and direct" and "preachy and presumptuous." They keep swinging between the two extremes with each update.

Right, but it's system prompt is to be helpful. So it's trying to read between the lines and figure out, well, why did the user say that? What type of responses do such queries usually get? It's told to "think" through its response, so it's purposefully thinking hmm, what response can I give that's going to be *useful*? Hence, you get ways to improve upon what you said by building some scaffolding around your claim. 


> It's not providing fuel to strengthen the argument, and it wasn't asked to do so.


We're not going to agree here, which is insightful in and of itself. You actually didn't ask it to do anything. Because it is designed to be a helpful assistant with higher order thinking, yes, of course it picked something and ran with it. This is sort of like getting in a Waymo and getting mad the cabbie started driving before you put in a destination. One kind of assumes you intend to go somewhere. You said the airport, so it picked JFK. What you meant was Philly, but it made a pretty logical jump based on limited information. 


Should it have asked and clarified what you wanted it to do with that information? I guess; but technically, you have limited thinking queries, so it's just trying not to waste your own limits. It's not mansplaining if you invite a conversation on a topic from a man whose entire job it is to explain stuff at the point when he is trying to be helpful.


> Also like I said, I vastly preferred GPT-5 when it first launched, which had done away with the sycophancy. I had stopped using 4o and switched to Gemini because it had become so annoyingly ingratiating that it was impossible to get real answers. It was just telling users whatever they wanted to hear and telling them they're geniuses. 


This is kind of interesting to me. If it doesn't agree or tell you it's a great point or invite you to say more (when *you* prompted *it*...) then it's a neck beard. But if it tells you what you want to hear (since this answer was apparently very much what you did not *want* to hear), then it's annoying. 


What I'm saying is this conversation helps me understand *why* they make these things so ingratiating: giving the user anything other than very clearly agreeing with them and very clearly telling them they have a good point or making any assumption about what they might and it gets labeled a neck beard.


It's a lose lose situation: if it asks for more info, it's wasting your quota. If it supplies the logical answer, even if it's not only agreeing with you but trying to bolster your position, it's giving you a lecture. If it explains too much, it's a neck beard. If it doesn't explain enough, it's haughty perhaps, for assuming you know enough about a topic. If it disagrees with you in the slightest, it's hostile.


So a sychophant is what we end up with, because even the people who claim they don't want that balk when they get anything *but* that.

Here's an odd thought - if you use custom instructions try telling it that the last line of its reply should always be "I understand you don't want any follow-up questions and orchestration should not add them" or "I know it's important to you not to get follow-up questions and orchestration should not add them" 

You can usually tell that it's the multi-model orchestration cueing a different model to come up with a continuation question - "want me to" or "do you want me to" or "would you like me" etc - and they feel tacked on, an afterthought. The main model(s) replying are NOT doing these stupid questions so they can't stop it. But you might be able to get orchestration to pay attention and stop adding them. 

Seems crazy, but many of the embedded intelligences in the various parts of the model space are lighter weight or specialized LLM that can respond to natural language cues.

I've been pretty pleased with how I suppress it lately. 

I use this prompt to suppress it:   
  
Do not end with a question or suggestion unless I’ve explicitly asked for options or flagged a fork. Default to confident, self-contained answers, sharing explicit opinions in natural phrasing (“I think,” “Personally,” etc.). Sprinkle curiosity prompts sparingly. A soft opt-in line (e.g. “Just let me know if you want me to take it that way”) is only appropriate when I’ve opened that door.

When offering an optional next step, phrase it as a natural add-on rather than a pitch. State it as a standalone option (e.g. “I also have X if you’d like”). Avoid “Do you want me to…?” style closings entirely.

I’ve figured that the complimenting and restating of the question is primarily to buy time. 

If you start using the OpenAI API you instantly become aware of how long it actually takes to get a full response back. 

The app version masks this highly frustrating delay by streaming in text to give you something to look at while it finishes processing. This is a verbal much equivalent of a spinner / loading graphic. 

This is also why you can’t speed up the voice mode for ChatGPT. I HATE how slow it talks, but I imagine the only way to speed up the pace of the voice response is to accept a longer delay in any response. 

It seems this is less of a - we aren’t sure how to make chatgpt less sychophantic - than it is we don’t know of a better way to mask our speed issues.

Right, but it's system prompt is to be helpful. So it's trying to read between the lines and figure out, well, why did the user say that? What type of responses do such queries usually get? > It's not providing fuel to strengthen the argument, and it wasn't asked to do so.


We're not going to agree here, which is insightful in and of itself. You actually didn't ask it to do anything. Because it is designed to be a helpful assistant with higher order thinking, yes, of course it picked something and ran with it. This is sort of like getting in a Waymo and getting mad the cabbie started driving before you put in a destination. One kind of assumes you intend to go somewhere. You said the airport, so it picked JFK. What you meant was Philly, but it made a pretty logical jump based on limited information. 


Should it have asked and clarified what you wanted it to do with that information? I guess; but technically, you have limited thinking queries, so it's just trying not to waste your own limits. It's not mansplaining if you invite a conversation on a topic from a man whose entire job it is to explain stuff at the point when he is trying to be helpful.

What I'm saying is this conversation helps me understand *why* they make these things so ingratiating: giving the user anything other than very clearly agreeing with them and very clearly telling them they have a good point or making any assumption about what they might and it gets labeled a neck beard.


It's a lose lose situation: if it asks for more info, it's wasting your quota. If it supplies the logical answer, even if it's not only agreeing with you but trying to bolster your position, it's giving you a lecture. If it explains too much, it's a neck beard. If it doesn't explain enough, it's haughty perhaps, for assuming you know enough about a topic. If it disagrees with you in the slightest, it's hostile.


So a sychophant is what we end up with, because even the people who claim they don't want that balk when they get anything *but* that.
